claims.text: LeetCode 322 gives coin denominations and a target amount, asks for the fewest coins needed, returns -1 when no combination can make the amount, and permits unlimited use of each denomination. Its examples include [1,2,5],11 -> 3; [2],3 -> -1; and [1],0 -> 0.

The candidate defines dp[x] as the minimum number of coins that exactly makes x, uses dp[0]=0, and minimizes dp[x-coin]+1 over usable positive denominations. The Java implementation matches an independent BFS shortest-path oracle on 961 generated cases covering every non-empty subset of {1,2,3,4,5} and amounts 0..30, in addition to all official examples.

Under the official positive-denomination contract, amount+1 is a valid unreachable sentinel because any reachable amount uses at most amount coins. The implementation fills amount states and scans every denomination for each, supporting O(amount * coins.length) time and O(amount) auxiliary space. Null and negative-amount handling are repository-local defensive extensions, not official input cases.

checks: all 961 cases from non-empty subsets of {1,2,3,4,5} and amounts 0..30 against an independent BFS shortest-path oracle

findings: The candidate matches the official LeetCode 322 minimum-coin contract, unlimited-use semantics, examples, and positive-denomination boundary.
The DP state, initialization, recurrence, amount iteration order, and unreachable-state handling are internally consistent.
The amount+1 sentinel is justified by the positive-integer denomination contract rather than used as an unexplained magic value.
The stated time and auxiliary-space bounds match the implementation.
The reproducible validation uses a structurally different BFS oracle across 961 generated cases, not just examples.
The answer explicitly distinguishes Coin Change from Coin Change II and avoids fabricated project experience.
